pl-l4d19c2-d1e115.summary: Quotes Augustine to show that a priest, even if bad, transmits grace by the office of his dignity: the Lord told Moses and Aaron 'put my name on the children of Israel, and I will bless them', so the tradition through the ordained minister transmits grace, and the priest's will can neither harm nor help, but the merit of the one asking. The dignity of priestly office is seen in the wicked Caiaphas, who prophesied as high priest, showing that the Spirit of graces follows not the person, worthy or unworthy, but the order, so that a good man cannot bless as minister unless ordained; the effect of blessing belongs to God.
claims: Grace passes through the ordained minister regardless of his worthiness.
The Spirit follows the order, not the person.
An unordained good man cannot bless as minister.

pl-l4d19c2-d1e136.summary: Concludes that the order is not deprived of the power of conferring grace by the minister's unworthiness.
claims: The minister's unworthiness does not void the order's power.

pl-l4d19c2-d1e139.summary: Objects with Hesychius: priests do not bless by their own power but because they bear Christ's figure and for him who is in them give the fullness of blessing; and not only one who has the priesthood but whoever has Christ in himself and bears his figure by good life, like Moses, is fit to give blessing.
claims: Hesychius: whoever bears Christ by good life can bless.

pl-l4d19c2-d1e146.summary: Draws out that here not only the priest but everyone in whom Christ dwells gives blessing.

pl-l4d19c2-d1e149.summary: Answers that one blessing belongs to priests alone, another is given in common by all the good. Priests in whom Christ dwells are said to give the fullness of blessing not because only they transmit grace, but because only they do so lawfully and worthily. A priest's bad life does not harm his subjects if they do the good he says.
claims: Priestly blessing differs from the blessing of all the good.
Good priests bless lawfully and worthily.
A bad priest's life does not harm his subjects.

pl-l4d19c2-d1e152.summary: Quotes Gregory: many, examining priests' lives more than their own, fall into error, not considering that priests' lives would not harm them if they listened humbly to their good admonitions.
claims: Judging priests' lives rather than heeding their teaching leads to error.

pl-l4d19c2.summary: Shows from Augustine that a priest, even if bad, transmits grace by virtue of his office: God told Moses and Aaron to put his name on Israel and he would bless them, so the ordained minister's tradition transmits grace, the priest's will neither harming nor helping but the merit of the one asking; even Caiaphas prophesied as high priest, since the Spirit follows not the person but the order, and an unordained good man cannot bless as a minister. Hesychius seems opposed, saying anyone who has Christ and bears his image by good life, like Moses, can bless. Lombard distinguishes the blessing proper to priests from that common to all the good; priests in whom Christ dwells give its fullness not because only they transmit grace but because only they do so lawfully and worthily. A bad priest's life does not harm his subjects who do the good he teaches, as Gregory says.
claims: A bad priest still transmits grace by virtue of his order.
The Spirit follows the order, not the person's worthiness.
Priestly blessing is distinct from blessing common to all the good.
Good priests confer blessing lawfully and worthily, bad ones validly.
A bad priest's life does not harm subjects who follow his good teaching.
